#8751. An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

Karen Sparks didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer.

This story was originally published in June 2021.

There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she says. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that plan, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

On the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

He’s killing my kids, she said, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

Her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”

It was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

She did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The plan was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

Two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

She discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up quickly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

She could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

Karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage company where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

Karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

To understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

Her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, big laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

She bought the gown at one of those big bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

The newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

David had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

After the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

Some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

Also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

It was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

That startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

She pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

The fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

How he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

Karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

Halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

Was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

The texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

Her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

From what Karen can piece together, it seems his plan was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

Was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

The fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

On November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

Somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Big Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who showed up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

She’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she plans to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

It will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she says, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

#8750. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

I’m sure I could think of a couple of thousand ways, many of which include espresso, to spend a Sunday morning in New York City than running 26.2 miles through all five boroughs. But on Nov. 1, nearly 60,000 people decided to run the New York City Marathon—again—like they have every year since 1970. Some were chasing a championship. Some were chasing a personal best. Others probably just wanted to finish before their feet decided to go on strike. And there are hosts of runners dressed in all kinds of costumes just out for a jog. And the crowd keeps everyone well cheered on. No matter who it is.

The men’s winner was Andreas Almgren of Sweden, who covered the course in two hours, six minutes, one second. And I’m going to put an asterisk next to it because this was his first marathon. Not his first race, obviously. Almgren arrived as the reigning world half-marathon champion and European 10,000-meter champion. He’d spent years developing the engine. He just hadn’t taken it out for this particular 26.2-mile test drive.

The lead pack stayed together deep into the race, and Almgren waited until the final mile to make his decisive move. Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa finished second, thirteen seconds behind him, and Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third. Defending champion Benson Kipruto wound up fourth. That’s quite a debut, particularly on a course that includes bridges, hills, crazy potholes and enough turns to get you lost.

Before anybody decides the lesson is to skip marathon preparation, understand what a debut means here. Almgren wasn’t some guy who woke up last Thursday and discovered running shoes. He had world-class credentials at shorter distances. Moving up required applying an already extraordinary aerobic foundation to a longer event. A marathon is not merely two half-marathons stapled together. Fueling, pacing, muscular endurance, and how you respond after mile twenty all become rather important when your body starts negotiating terms of surrender.

The women’s race was even more entertaining near the finish. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui reclaimed the title she’d won in 2024, finishing in 2:24:36. Defending champion Hellen Obiri was in the fight late, but American Jess McClain came charging from behind and passed her in the closing meters. Chepkirui won, McClain took second in 2:24:42, and Obiri was third one second later. McClain became the first American woman on the New York podium since 2018.

And if you think the only interesting athletes are the ones with the smallest numbers on the clock, the wheelchair divisions cranks them out! Switzerland’s Marcel Hug won his eighth New York title in 1:28:14, edging American Daniel Romanchuk by one second. Catherine Debrunner, also Swiss, won the women’s wheelchair race in 1:40:02, nearly eight and a half minutes ahead of Tatyana McFadden. Same city, same event, completely different demands on the athlete. The upper-body power, equipment handling, and tactical judgment involved deserve more attention than they usually get.

Then there’s Mildred Baker, an 80-year-old Bronx resident who took up running in her late seventies and completed her first marathon in 7:03:49. Seven freakin’ hours! No, Almgren is not the only champion. That’s the point. The marathon can be a world championship-level knife fight at the front and a personal expedition at the back. And a trade in between. You can appreciate both extremes without pretending they’re the same athletic achievement.

Secondly, I must admit that l like the way this race exposes a certain kind of gym stupidity: the assumption that only one type of physical performance counts. A Swedish speed merchant conquered a distance he’d never raced. An American woman stole second place in the final strides. An 80-year-old finished something most people wouldn’t even start. You’re actually, in one Sunday event, looking at the entire definition of fitness.

The S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#8746. Bodybuilder AJ Ellison Shares 3 tips for Fat Loss After 50

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

IFBB Pro and Masters Men’s Physique Competitor Adam J. Ellison may be 50 years old, but he has a physique that would make most men half his age green with envy. Fortunately, the proud father of three kids says that it is still possible to drop fat while juggling the responsibilities of work and family, as he shared his “No B.S. guide” on Instagram.

AJ Ellison knows that fat mass tends to increase while lean muscle decreases with age, and science suggests that the slow down in metabolic rates could play a significant role as to why it is harder to drop body fat as we age, but that doesn’t mean that we should ditch our physique goals  as we mature. Ellison, now 50 years old, is still winning competitions on stage, and looked phenomenal as he topped the Master’s 50+ Men’s Physique category at the 2026 IFBB Masters World Championships. He even placed second in the 40+, meaning that AJ is still hanging with those who are up to a decade younger than himself. With all that in mind, here are his tips for dropping stubborn fat.

“Fat loss doesn’t start in the gym, it starts in your kitchen,” wrote Ellison. “You can’t out-train a poor diet.” The big man also said that he makes sure to consume plenty of protein. “Aim for 50 to 70g of protein at every meal. Build every plate around protein first. Fill the rest with whole foods.”

“Most men try to burn more calories. That’s backwards,” said Ellison. “Protect your muscle first.” While muscle does not burn calories directly, the presence of more muscle tissue means that there is a greater level of energy required in the body, leading to a greater calorie requirement.

To build muscle, the competitive bodybuilder suggested that we “Lift 3 to 4 times every week,” and added that for hypertrophy, “Progress your lifts whenever possible.”

“Cardio is a tool. It isn’t the foundation,” believes Ellison, who utilizes cardiovascular training to support his efforts without making it the center of his ethos. “Strength training should always come first,” wrote the master, for his almost 900K Instagram followers.

To make sure that cardio is part of the mix, “Add 8,000 to 10,000 daily steps,” enthused Ellison. “Use cardio to support recovery, not to punish yourself.”

Summing up, the bodybuilder noted that “Small calorie deficits beat aggressive diets,” observing that “Crash dieting teaches your body to conserve energy.” So, to get started, Ellison coached that we should aim to lose 0.5 to 1% of body fat per week, and to trust in the process. “Track your progress for at least three weeks before changing anything,” he concluded.

#8743. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

As it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

South Mountain has a lot longer trails to hike on too (College Ave has a bike/ped bridge over the highway so it’s easy to get to). I would suggest going to Prescott AZ first, because it’s almost as beautiful naturally and far nicer as a town, with a great walkable downtown. I’m all for adventuring to different places and trying to things – but I’m not “getting it” about the culdesac being innovative and new. AnotherEngineer November 3, 2023, 12:57 pm

I don’t know the details of culdesac, but much of what you say is fair in general. Our development system is quite broken as it depends on risk-adverse, profit-seeking developers to build out a communities’ land use vision, which may or may not be supportive of car-lite living in itself. It has resulted in sprawl and “luxury” everything sameness and widespread auto dependence. I agree ideally there would be lots of employment in the development, but I would argue that dense, transit accessible housing is the greater need in our system. Less regulation is often the answer here (e.g., removing parking minimums, increasing residential zoning density), but in your example, clearly some way of ensuring that the development follows through on its promises it made for approval is needed. On the flip side, any housing built, even if it is for AirBnbs is creating housing and likely converting other short term to long term rentals due to competition. Any dense housing in an area that isn’t car dependent is a win in my book, and culdesac’s ideals seem about as good as a developer of a single parcel can do to prove a concept and get the ball rolling. I hope they are vey successful and make lots of money to prove the concept elsewhere, which can translate into lower price points, mixed use, 15 minute cities, etc.

If you have significant savings, you’ll probably have a history of tax returns that show your dividend and other investment income, which is probably fine for renting at any reasonable apartment complex. I’ve been able to do this even to get mortgages in these post-retirement years.

Offering to pay multiple months is a good strategy too. If someone doesn’t want your money, move on down the road.

I’ve often wondered about the problem of renting when one doesn’t have a “job”. I am going to be selling my house this spring (after 40 years), and am planning to rent moving forward. I just assumed that providing a landlord with documented income information via tax returns would be enough to prove one’s income stream. The irony is that ever since I retired, I make more money per annum that I ever did while working, due to lucky investments along the way that generate income. Once the house is cashed in, the residual income from the invested funds will generate more monthly income than most renters earn through employment. So the “you can’t rent without a job” really makes no sense at all. Unless the landlord or property management company are total morons.

I know this is a few days late, but if you see it, there is also qualifying based on assets. I’m not working and my hubby is doing a fun but shittily paid Americorps job, so we couldn’t qualify on income. Fortunately, the agent asked about assets and we qualified that way.

When we previously lived in Alexandria, they also wouldn’t let you pay upfront. Didn’t make sense to me, but that was the policy. You also might have better luck with an individual landlord than a property company. I had a friend who paid for 2 whole years in advance in Philly a few years ago.

It’s so funny you mention Dopamine Nation because just yesterday I was discussing that book with a friend and how it reminded me of your philosophy of voluntary hardship. It’s fascinating to explore the science behind boosting your dopamine by doing intentionally hard things. Since reading the book, I’ve been experimenting with little changes like cold showers, increasing my weights at the gym, and eating for nourishment instead of entertainment. :)

I recently read that book after hearing the author interviewed by both Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman. It gave me a new perspective on motivation and “happiness”, and closed the loop on these ideas as so practically described by MMM. Satisfaction, contentment, and motivation come to us by way of the “struggle” and the the effort of dealing with and facing challenging situations of all sorts – physical, emotional, and mental. Feeding our desires constantly – eating, entertainment, alcohol, drugs, shopping, etc. – only serve to make us less and less happy and more and more depressed. Eliminating our cravings and desires, while pursuing intentional hardships to keep us fit, sharp, and strong, ultimates results in a more satisfying state of mind and a fulfilling sense of wellbeing. It all comes together with the MMM philosophy of living a simple, frugal, productive, and healthy lifestyle.

While you’re in Arizona, you may want to check out Arcosanti, about half way between Phoenix and Sedona. It’s the original attempt at a prototype arcology, the 1960s urban planning model defined by Paolo Soleri and later popularized in Sim City and many science fiction novels. He focussed on combining dense urban living, environmental conservation, and place-based architecture. Arcosanti is itself beautiful, and it’s fascinating to see how the ideas that germinated there have slowly been manifesting in places like Culdesac.

Hmm, yeah that is indeed a bit too personal for this comments section (I do my best not to mix my relationship life with the MMM Internet life – except for that one necessary mention that we amicably parted ways in 2018).

But I do like to share a general message, because divorce is such a common thing yet it is widely associated with shame and blame: it is OKAY if it’s right for you. It’s not a failure or a negative, selfish choice. And more people need to get over the fear of making changes like that in their lives, once they have done their best to think it through. And more people need to be nice about it as they go through the process.

I think I’m a long-term-couple person at the core, so I happily look forward to settling down in that way in my own future. But as with any relationship, both people need to be compatible and appreciative with each other. And as an outrageous optimist, I believe there ARE plenty of wonderful people out there for everyone!

We left the desert as (in our opinion) there isn’t enough water in the West to meet the ever-growing demand. We are also older now (late 60s) and an 8+ hour drive (round-trip) for cancer treatments made us very aware of the downside of wide-open spaces. Winter weather is great, but in the summer you really can’t exercise outside later than 10 am. That said, I love the idea of this community. I hope it succeeds and many more are built across the country. Enjoy your time in AZ!

Welcome to AZ. Just to set your expectations post Summer; you won’t be leaving.

HEY! Look at that! All my worlds are colliding!

I’m a fellow Canadian (Newfoundlander to be precise) who’s been reading your blog from the very beginning. Mostly it’s a case of “preaching to the converted”.

I’ve been spending winters in Arizona for the last 10 years because my partner (also from Newfoundland) lives in Chandler. And literally, no joke, the first item that I have written down on my list of things to do in Arizona this coming winter is “go check out Cul De Sac”.

Maybe if I go and wander around there, I’ll spot your facial hair

I don’t know if it’s weird to say this, but I’d be up for a coffee or a bike ride or some hang time or whatever if you feel so inclined. It would definitely be the weirdest way that I’ve ever made a friend. In a good way.

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

Hey MMM, my wife’s been following you for a long time and told me you were moving out to Tempe. I grew up there, and still meet up with friends I’ve known in the area since elementary school. Tempe’s a great college town- Go Sun Devils!

I live in east Mesa now, close to Usery Mountain National Park and the Superstition Mountains. I’m a retired teacher, solar guy, and artist. I do a lot of hiking and biking in the area, as well as SUP and kayaking. If you and your son would like a tour guide/hiking/biking/river partner, be sure and get in touch.

#8741. Stephan James Cut Weight in Order to Look Bigger for ‘I Play Rocky’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.
